extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students, researchers, and interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style exposition of the Four Color Theorem: definitions, precise formulation in graph-theoretic terms, historical proof attempts, the computer-assisted proofs (Appel–Haken, Robertson et al., Gonthier), proof ideas (triangulation, reducible configurations, unavoidable sets, discharging), and generalizations to other surfaces and infinite graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacency definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjacent means that two regions share a common boundary of non-zero length (i.e., not merely a corner where three or more regions meet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If shared only at an isolated point (a corner) the regions are not considered adjacent; otherwise a pie-chart-type map could force arbitrarily many 'adjacencies' and require arbitrarily many colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed region shapes / map regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bizarre regions, such as those with finite area but infinitely long perimeter, are not allowed; to be safe, restrict to regions whose boundaries consist of finitely many straight line segments. It is allowed that a region has enclaves (entirely surrounds one or more other regions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps with pathological regions can require more than four colors; this restriction ensures the informal statement of the theorem is meaningful in the usual cartographic sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-theoretic formulation (planar graph requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four-color theorem can be stated in graph-theoretic terms: for a loopless planar graph G, denoting by χ(G) its chromatic number, χ(G) ≤ 4. Represent each region by a vertex and draw an edge for every pair of regions that share a boundary segment; conversely every planar graph arises this way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence allows proofs and algorithms to be stated in graph-theoretic language rather than in terms of geographic regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contiguous-region vs country/exclave caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of 'contiguous region' (technically: connected open subset of the plane) is not the same as that of 'country' on regular maps, since a country may have exclaves; if one requires the entire territory of a country to receive the same color, then four colors are not always sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given where two disconnected parts of the same country forced a fifth color; thus the theorem applies to connected regions, not to arbitrary sets of regions that must share color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: If planar regions are not triangulated (do not have exactly three edges in their boundaries), one can add edges without introducing new vertices to make every region triangular; it suffices to prove the four color theorem for triangulated graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coloring of the triangulated graph remains valid when added edges are removed, so proving the theorem for triangulations implies it for all planar graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal counterexample concept and basic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a graph requiring 5 colors exists, consider a minimal such graph G where removing any vertex makes it four-colorable. Such a minimal G cannot have a vertex of degree 3 or less (since removal and re-addition extend the coloring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimality argument underpins reduction strategies: proving that no minimal counterexample can exist yields the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kempe chains and recoloring technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A Kempe chain is an alternating path of vertices colored with two colors (e.g., red-blue). Recoloring along a Kempe chain can allow extending a four-coloring when re-adding a removed vertex (this works for the degree-4 case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kempe used this method successfully for degree 4; however his overall proof failed because the degree-5 case was handled incorrectly. The technique remains a basic recoloring tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration and reducible configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: A configuration is a connected subgraph of G with the degree of each vertex (in G) specified. A reducible configuration is an arrangement of countries that cannot occur in a minimal counterexample because if the configuration is removed and the remaining graph four-colored, the coloring can be modified so the four-coloring extends to the configuration when it is re-added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The configuration's ring (vertices adjacent to the configuration) and ringed configuration are used to enumerate ring colorings. An 'initially good' ring-coloring extends without modification; otherwise systematic recoloring is required (this is the principal step where computer assistance is needed due to the large number of cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unavoidable set
rubrics_metrics.description: An unavoidable set is a set of configurations such that every map that satisfies the necessary conditions for being a minimal non-4-colorable triangulation must contain at least one configuration from this set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one can exhibit an unavoidable set all of whose members are reducible, then a minimal counterexample cannot exist and the theorem follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of discharging
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign each vertex of degree i an initial charge of 6−i, then redistribute ('discharge') charge among vertices according to a set of rules that preserve total charge. Because the total is initially positive, some vertices remain positively charged; the discharging rules constrain which configurations of positively charged vertices can occur, enabling enumeration of an unavoidable set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discharging is intuitively described as treating the planar graph as an electrical network; the choice and complexity of discharging rules are central to producing a manageable unavoidable set (Appel–Haken's rules were extremely complex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ringed configuration color enumeration and 'initially good' colorings
rubrics_metrics.description: For a configuration, the surrounding vertices form a ring; enumerate all distinct four-colorings of the ring. Any coloring that can be extended without modification to a coloring of the configuration is called 'initially good'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the large number of ring colorings, testing whether every ring coloring is either initially good or convertible to one is the main computationally intensive part of reducibility checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersion reducibility (technical requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immersion reducibility is a technical detail required to complete the proof (mentioned as a necessary notion beyond the basic reducibility concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes this as a technical point without elaboration; it functions as an additional reducibility condition used in formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for computer-assisted proof verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Appel and Haken reduced the problem to a finite (originally 1,834, later 1,482) list of reducible configurations to be checked by computer; reducibility checks were run on different programs/computers and independently double-checked. Later work produced shorter lists (633 configurations) and a Coq formalization (Gonthier) that mechanized the whole proof inside a proof assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because much of the proof relies on machine checking, independent verification, transparency of algorithms, and, ideally, formalization in a trusted proof assistant were important for acceptance. The Coq formalization shifts trust to the proof assistant kernel rather than ad hoc programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-coloring complexity and cubic-map criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: While every planar map can be colored with four colors, deciding whether an arbitrary planar map can be colored with just three colors is NP-complete. A cubic map can be colored with only three colors iff each interior region has an even number of neighboring regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a precise hardness statement and a special-case necessary-and-sufficient condition for cubic maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization to other surfaces (Heawood formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: For closed surfaces of positive genus, the maximum number p of colors needed depends on the Euler characteristic χ of the surface. Except for the Klein bottle, p = floor((7 + sqrt(49−24χ))/2). For orientable surfaces this can be expressed in terms of genus g: p = floor((7 + sqrt(1+48g))/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Heawood formula (proved by Ringel and Youngs) gives the chromatic upper bound for surfaces; the Klein bottle is the only exception (requires six colors rather than the formula's seven). Examples: torus needs at most seven colors; Möbius strip requires six.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to infinite graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: The four-color theorem applies to infinite graphs that can be drawn without crossings in the plane, and more generally to infinite graphs (possibly uncountable) for which every finite subgraph is planar. This follows by combining the finite theorem with the De Bruijn–Erdős theorem or via Gödel's compactness theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement reduces the infinite case to the finite case by compactness/finite-subgraph arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to extend to 3-dimensional solid regions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no obvious extension of the coloring result to three-dimensional solid regions: one can arrange n folded rods or axis-parallel cuboids so that every piece touches every other piece, forcing an unbounded number of colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows that adjacency-based coloring bounds that hold in the plane do not generalize to higher dimensions; concrete constructions (rods, cuboids) yield arbitrarily large chromatic requirements.
